title: Hidden-debt revelations create a transparency shock that reprices sovereign risk and fiscal room
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11462, Sovereign Risk Repricing after Hidden-Debt Revelations
geography: Seven sovereign hidden-debt revelation episodes during 2005-2025: Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Mozambique, Pakistan, Senegal, Türkiye, and Zambia

observations.period: Seven hidden-debt revelations; first 60 days after each revelation

denominator.unit: country episodes in the event-study sample

first_30_days.value: pooled sovereign risk spreads rise 108 basis points on average during the first 30 days

first_10_days.value: 66 basis points of the first-30-day increase occurs in the first 10 days

days_31_60.value: spreads rise by an additional 98 basis points during days 31-60

repricing_mechanism.value: markets reassess repayment risk and fiscal sustainability when previously undisclosed liabilities become public

observations.method: Daily sovereign risk spread event study around seven hidden-debt revelations, with alternative specifications used as robustness checks.
observations.uncertainty: The sample contains only seven episodes; spread movements can also reflect contemporaneous macroeconomic, political, commodity, or global-risk shocks, although the paper reports robust baseline results.
observations.subgroup: Borrowing governments, domestic taxpayers, public-service users, creditors, firms dependent on public contracts, and households exposed to later fiscal adjustment.
observations.counterinterpretation: A spread increase is a market-risk measure; it does not by itself establish a subsequent default, austerity package, decline in public services, or realized household welfare loss.

observations.period: Hidden-debt revelations with different reconciliation trajectories; 60 days after revelation

denominator.unit: country episodes available for suggestive heterogeneity analysis

contested_reconciliation.value: when debt reconciliation is delayed or contested, sovereign spreads rise roughly 200 basis points more over 60 days than when reconciliation is prompt

information_persistence.value: uncertainty about the full scope of undisclosed obligations can keep spreads elevated for longer

governance_signal.value: repricing reflects not only the newly measured debt stock but also market inference about borrowing-country governance and transparency

trust_route.value: the credibility of disclosure and reconciliation becomes part of the fiscal signal evaluated by external markets

observations.method: Event-study comparison of spread paths by whether debt reconciliation was prompt versus delayed or contested.
observations.uncertainty: The paper labels this result suggestive because the number of episodes is small; reconciliation categories may also bundle differences in politics, institutions, debt composition, and revelation size.
observations.subgroup: Government auditors, finance ministries, legislatures, creditors, rating and market participants, firms, and citizens evaluating fiscal credibility.
observations.counterinterpretation: The result does not prove that a single communication strategy restores trust or that disclosure automatically lowers borrowing costs; substantive fiscal correction and institutional credibility may matter jointly.

observations.period: Sovereign borrowing and downstream fiscal adjustment after hidden-debt revelation

denominator.unit: transmission chain tested as an analytical boundary rather than a household-level estimate

fiscal_room.value: higher sovereign spreads mechanically raise the cost of refinancing and can narrow future fiscal room

public_system_route.value: any later effects on public services, transfers, taxes, procurement, or infrastructure require a separate country-level follow-through test

political_attribution.value: the revelation can convert hidden liabilities into a visible contest over responsibility, disclosure, and who bears adjustment costs

consumer_household_route.value: household consumption and security may be affected only through subsequent fiscal, price, employment, or service changes not measured in this paper

observations.method: Cross-domain interpretation of the paper's sovereign-spread result, with explicit separation between observed market repricing and unobserved social outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: The paper does not estimate household welfare, service delivery, tax incidence, political legitimacy, or firm behavior after each revelation; the downstream chain is a testable research agenda, not a measured effect here.
observations.subgroup: Households with different tax, transfer, employment, and service dependencies; firms reliant on public finance; and political groups contesting responsibility for hidden obligations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Governments may absorb or refinance the higher cost without immediate service cuts, and later reforms may improve transparency or fiscal resilience; direction and distribution of downstream effects are country-specific.

related_sources.claim: Official World Bank record, authors, date, WPS number, abstract, and reproducibility link.
Bibliographic record and abstract reporting the 108 basis-point and additional 98-basis-point estimates and suggestive reconciliation heterogeneity.
World Bank reproducibility package and verification metadata.
World Bank Global Economic Prospects discussion of hidden-debt revelations, persistent spread increases, governance/transparency inference, and fiscal implications.

boundary: This record adds a transparency-to-sovereign-risk repricing mechanism. It is an event-study of market spreads across seven episodes, not evidence that hidden-debt revelations directly caused household welfare loss, public-service decline, austerity, default, or political legitimacy change. Those downstream cultural, social, consumer, and political effects require named country follow-through sources.
